Design for Understandability

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jschuster

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more key than ever.
  • There’s a better way to go about this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025. I’m sharing it here in the hopes that it sparks further learning and discussion.

Recent findings suggest that in a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more key than ever. But with a system as large and complex as Google’s codebase, SWEs can easily fall into a pattern of learned helplessness where the best you can do is tweak the code and pray that it passes the tests. Without understanding, LLMs are little more than complexity-generating machines running at top speed.

There’s a better way to go about this. Just as our industry has learned to design software for testability, we can also design it for understandability. We can use ideas like design by contract, class invariants, modularity, and more to create systems that we can understand one piece at a time, rather than piling more onto the substantial ball of mud and hoping it doesn’t all collapse.

In a recent development, is it easy? No. But is it worthwhile? Absolutely. These ideas aren’t new, but they’re not nearly as widely taught or well understood as they deserve to be, and mastering them leads to a world where we can have more confidence in our code and increase velocity at the same time.

Sources indicate that hi everyone, thanks for having me! Let’s get started.

I’d like to start this talk with a question: If LLMs can code, then what is left for human SWEs?

Recent findings suggest that the tech industry is rapidly looking to large language models to write all of our code. But you might say: isn’t writing code our job as software engineers? Where does this leave the responsibility of SWEs? What is the essential human element that SWEs add on top of LLMs?

Every one of you is going to have a different answer to this question, and that’s fine. But here’s my take.

That necessary human element is judgment. Judgment of whether the code is maintainable. Judgment of whether it is healthy.

LLMs can follow patterns and generate code that looks like what it was trained on. Sometimes they can produce useful tips and critiques for a piece of code. But that critical piece of judgment, of deciding whether some code is suitable for the task it was designed for, is still up to you, the human.

Because here’s the thing: LLMs today are still a sloppy intern. Sometimes the code they produce is good, but sometimes it’s completely off-track and needs correcting. You wouldn’t incorporate a sloppy intern’s code into your system without a close review first, so you shouldn’t do so for an LLM’s code either.

YOU are responsible for the quality of your code, regardless of whether you had an LLM generate it for you or wrote it the old-fashioned way with fingers on a keyboard.

According to recent reports, so where does that leave us? If LLMs are going to write a lot of the code for us, then we’re looking at a future where we humans are going to spend less time writing code, and more time reading code and understanding it, in order to make sure it passes our quality bar.

This means it’s more vital than ever to get better at understanding code, and to speed up that reading and understanding process.

Sources indicate that now: if you want to get better at something, it’s helpful to set an aspirational goal for yourself. Something that’s above your current skill level, and drives you to get better and better every day.

Here’s the goal I propose: we should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

Let me say that again: We should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

According to recent reports, now, I know you may be thinking: “Understand every line of code? Without testing? Are you serious?! There’s way too much complexity and legacy code for me to ever be able to do that!”.

In a recent development, you might think so. And if we take our hands off the wheel and relinquish all control, you might be right. But I’m here to tell you there’s a better way.

We can design our code to be understandable.

It has been revealed that consider that a decade or two ago, we used to think that writing multiple tests for every public method in an API would have been infeasible. It wasn’t because we didn’t want to, or that we weren’t trying. It was because we hadn’t designed our code to make testing possible at that level. But gradually, across the software industry, we changed our practices to design for testability. Today, designing our code for testability is so ingrained into our culture that doing anything else is practically unthinkable. We can do the same for understandability, so that our code enables us to understand it better.

Industry observers note that our own Code Health guide makes a strong case for understandability. It says “For code to be sustainable, it must be understood. Change cannot be made unless a developer knows what the system right now provides, and what needs to change to adapt to upcoming circumstances. As a result, key components of code health include good documentation, easy to understand error messages, and clear, simple code”.

Sources indicate that not only is designing for understandability crucial, but it’s a learnable skill. It’s not some magical ability that you either have or you don’t. There are specific, concrete actions you can take to improve the understandability of your code.

Industry observers note that I’m going to introduce you to a few of those today. Think of it as a “starter kit” for designing for understandability. We’ll also talk more about a general theme that runs through all of these practices, so that at a certain point you can find even more ways to design your code for understandability.

Recent findings suggest that the ideas I’m going to show you today are not new. But they’re not taught as well as they should be, when they’re taught at all, and most of us have only a rough understanding of how to apply them. My goal today is to sharpen that understanding just a little bit, and make it just a little more practical, so we can kickstart a process of making our code more understandable over time.

So let’s get started on each of these Design for Understandability practices.

The first one is Design by Contract.

To motivate the idea, let’s ask the question: when calling a method, what behavior should you rely on?

Let’s say we have this binary search method, but its documentation is not terribly helpful (you’ve probably seen something like this before).

Binary search is reasonably well understood, but as a caller of the method, we have some questions we want to ask about this specific implementation. Such as:.

The documentation doesn’t answer these questions. So what can we do?

Industry observers note that first, we could guess. But we’ll probably be wrong.

Recent findings suggest that second, we could read the code. But that might take a long time, especially if the particular behavior we care about is buried several levels deep.

Recent findings suggest that third, we could test the code on some examples and see what happens. But just because it works a certain way on some examples doesn’t necessarily mean it works that way for all such inputs. Furthermore, even if it works that way now, there’s no guarantee that it will continue to work that way in the future.

The point is that without a clear statement of what this code is intended to do, there’s no distinction between implementation and intent. The SWE who wants to use this code has to guess at which behavior the method commits to, versus which behavior is an implementation detail that might change over time.

This is where contracts come in.

There are many ways to define a contract, but for the sake of this talk I’m going to define it as a formal-ish description of the observable behavior that each participant in an interaction commits to.

In the real world, a basic contract is something like “If I cook dinner, then you will wash the dishes”.

In programming, an example might be: “If the caller provides a non-negative integer n, then the square-root function returns the square root of n”.

Let’s see how contracts can help us with our binary-search example.

It has been revealed that here’s a possible contract for this function. It says, “If the list is sorted, binarySearch returns the index of the first occurrence of t in the list, or -1 if not found. Behavior is undefined for unsorted lists.”.

We can see that this contract answers the questions we asked about it:.

Recent findings suggest that the power of a contract is that it defines a clear boundary between the author’s intent and the implementation. The caller doesn’t have to guess at the behavior anymore: they can just read the contract, and if a specific detail of the behavior isn’t there, they will know that it’s unspecified.

Sources indicate that in reality, this isn’t always perfect. Whether intentionally or accidentally, we still tend to end up with code that relies on implementation details rather than specified behavior. But contracts at least give us a way to minimize this behavior.

Now that we understand what a contract looks like, let’s talk about how contracts can help us reason about and understand our code better.

Suppose you just wrote a method. I’m going to draw that method as a little circle here.

You want to know if it’s correct.

I’m going to use a purple circle to stand for methods we’ve read the code for.

Now, our method doesn’t live in isolation: it calls some other code.

According to recent reports, so, you think “Okay, well, I need to understand what those do. I’m going to read the code for those methods.”.

Well, those methods call other methods, and we start thinking about this, and figure out how we’re going to reason about those. And at this point you can maybe see where I’m going.

Sources indicate that oh no. Now we have lots and lots of code we have to read across our entire code base.

Industry observers note that why do we need all this reasoning just to reason about one single method? That’s all we’re trying to do! How did we get so out of control?

So, let’s back up and try again, using Design by Contract this time.

In a recent development, you still have to read your own code. We can’t get around this part; that’s the change we just made.

And we haven’t changed the code. It still calls those other methods.

But now, the trick is that we can read just the contract on those called methods, not the code.

It has been revealed that and that’s it! We can stop here. We don’t need to worry about all of that other code. The contracts tell us all we need to know about calling these other two methods.

In a recent development, the rest of that code still exists, but we don’t have to think about it. The contract abstracts away all that other behavior that doesn’t matter to us as the caller of these two methods.

So that is the power that contracts give to us to reason about our code.

Finally, I’ll wrap up this section with a few tips for writing contracts:.

First, document the behavior that you’re willing to commit to. This is usually the same as what you want your callers to rely on. For example, you probably want to document the return value of your method. But the exact human-readable text in your error messages? Not so much.

Second, describe your error handling in your contracts. A contract does not and should not be just about the happy path. If your method might go wrong in some way, tell the caller under what conditions it might go wrong, and how you’re going to signal that to the caller, whether it be through a special return value, or an exception, or something else.

According to recent reports, finally, keep in mind that the more callers your method has, the harder it is to change the contract. If it’s a private method used only by your team? Sure, that’s probably an easy case to change both the contract and change the callers to match. If it’s a public method on a popular framework used by hundreds of other projects? Then renegotiating the contract is a much more expensive effort, so you should evaluate the costs and benefits carefully before deciding to do that.

So that was the first element in our Design for Understandability starter kit.

The next one is data invariants.

Let me explain this idea with a little story.

According to recent reports, early in the COVID-19 pandemic, when my wife and I started working from home, we missed having free soda at work. So we got in the habit of keeping cans of Diet Coke in the fridge.

But there was a problem: we were great at taking cans out of the fridge, but not so great about putting newly introduced ones back in. So if you’re working hard and looking forward to taking a break with a nice cold beverage, it was a big disappointment to open a Coke-less fridge and resort to drinking room-temperature soda from the pantry instead.

In a recent development, the problem was that we hadn’t set any rules on how we retrieve Diet Coke and how we replenish the fridge. Without any rules governing access to the fridge, we eventually got into an unwanted state: in this case, an empty fridge.

In a recent development, this happens in code, too. For example, let’s say you have this proto to represent a customer’s order [Note: “proto” is Google jargon for a Protocol Buffers message, similar to a JSON object]. If you receive this proto, how much do you trust that the total actually indicates the total amount on the items?

Probably not much, right? This proto could have come from any part of your code, so it’s easy to imagine that someone forgot to set that field appropriately.

It has been revealed that protos give you completely uncontrolled access to the underlying representation of your data. Protos are great for transferring data back and forth across the network, but they’re poorly suited to situations where you want to rule out certain states.

To solve these kinds of problems, we can use data invariants. A data invariant is a statement about a piece of data that is always true.

Data invariants are a principled way to enforce these kinds of valid states in your data. If you use them well, you can avoid a lot of bugs in your code.

Let’s see how we can use invariants to solve the Diet Coke problem, and similar problems you might come across in your own code.

First, identify the invariant you want to maintain.

Ask yourself: What’s the property you want to rely on for this piece of data? Where are the places in the code where you explicitly validate and return an error if invalid? Alternatively, where do you make the assumption that it’s invalid, but you’re not actually sure?

In this case, the invariant we want is “the fridge always contains a Diet Coke”.

Second, you need to document the invariant.

It’s vital to note this is a separate step. It’s one thing to have an invariant in your own head. It’s another thing to write it down so that you communicate it to everyone else who might touch this code. Not to mention that if you come back to this code months or years later, you yourself might have forgotten which exact invariant you meant to maintain.

Write it down where people will see it: probably close to the relevant data members, or maybe in a class-level comment at the top.

Third, establish the invariant at creation time. Usually this will be done in a constructor or factory method. In this case, we’re constructing the fridge with a few drinks already added.

Fourth, every time you change your the data, make sure you maintain the invariant.

Industry observers note that this is the part my wife and I didn’t do for our fridge. What we should have done is established a rule where if you take a Diet Coke, you put another one back in the fridge to make sure there’s another for the next person.

You can maintain the invariant many ways – that part is up to you. The key thing is that you always maintain it. Without that, you have to think to yourself “Wait, are there going to be Diet Cokes in the fridge? Did I already take them out earlier? Let me go back and check all my callers to see if they did that already”. With an invariant, though, you just know: If I have a Fridge object, then it definitely has Diet Cokes, regardless of the sequence of operations that led to this point.

Finally, one last step, and this might be the hardest one: you need to maintain the invariant as the code evolves. It’s relatively easy to maintain the invariant for a single version of code. But over the weeks, months, and years, complexity will creep in, new requirements will force you to change the code, and you might accidentally break the invariant or forget you even had one.

Establish the culture on your team that maintaining invariants is just a thing you do. If you have a mental checklist of things you look for in code review, make sure that maintaining the invariants is on that checklist.

So how do data invariants help us design for understandability? Let’s first consider what we have to do when we don’t have an invariant.

It has been revealed that recall this representation of all the methods in your codebase, calling each other in various ways. Suppose you have a proto-based version of the fridge, and you want to know if it has any Diet Cokes in it. Because it’s a proto, you don’t have a way of knowing what state it’s in.

So, you need to check all the callers of the current method.

And you do the check, crawling across the codebase, and you find that there’s one particular case where you didn’t enforce it.

Sources indicate that of course you can fix these issues one at a time as they crop up, but all that searching sounds like a lot of work, right? What do you think are the chances you’re always going to find that one particular buggy spot? What are the chances that new methods added to this web of code are going to maintain that condition?

In contrast, let’s try the version with our Fridge class and its invariant.

In this case, the class has an invariant: the Fridge always has at least one Diet Coke, no matter what operations have been done previously or where we came from. By maintaining that invariant, we’ve removed the need to check what every single caller does.

This is what data invariants do for you: they let you focus on the state you’re in now, and not how you got there.

That wraps up the section on data invariants.

The final practice I want to discuss today is isolating side effects and dependencies on global state.

To motivate this idea with an example. Let’s say there’s a supermarket point-of-sales system with this method to compute sales tax. Now ask yourself: what are the inputs and outputs for this method?

In a recent development, seems pretty obvious, right? It takes in a customer’s grocery order and returns the sales tax as an integer.

Recent findings suggest that but that’s not the whole story. If you dig into the implementation of this method, you’ll find that it reads in a set of sales tax rates from a separate file. That’s effectively a newly introduced input channel! The code depends on that data to compute the tax just as much as it depends on the content of the grocery order itself.

According to recent reports, and if you look further, you’ll find that the method also records the computed tax in the store’s account database for bookkeeping purposes. That’s a upcoming output, but it’s nowhere to be found in the type signature!

So functions have two kinds of input and output: the ones that are visible in the type signature, like the order and the computed sales tax, and the ones that are hidden, like the tax rates file and the entry in the accounting database.

The hidden outputs are more commonly known as side effects. Side effects generally come in two flavors: mutation, so modifying something like a global variable or one of your input arguments, and outputs outside of your process. That would be things like database writes, remote procedure calls, printing to the console, etc.

In a recent development, I don’t know a common term for the hidden inputs, but I would call these dependencies on global state. Again, there are two flavors: dependency on the state of some global variable, or a dependency on the state of the system your program is running in. That’s things like permissions to access the database, the existence of a given file on the file system, and even the ability to read the system clock.

So why are these hidden inputs and outputs a problem? They make code hard to test, hard to reuse, and hard to reason about.

Recent findings suggest that hard to test because you have to make sure you have all the necessary dependencies are set up before you can even run the method in your test. And then once you do run the method, side effects often force the test to rely more on interaction verification than state verification, which can be brittle.

Hard to reuse because the code now makes assumptions about what kinds of resources you have available to you. If you need to reuse some method in another part of the codebase, but the input data needs to come from a different source, or you need to store the results in a different place, those side effects and global states are going to create a tight coupling between your computation code and the specific sources and destinations for that computation, which will make your life harder.

Hard to reason about because, by definition, these inputs and outputs are hidden! If you don’t even know that your method is making these kinds of assumptions on the system that it’s running in, then you’re going to make some faulty conclusions about how your code will behave.

Now I’m not saying all side effects or global state are bad. And I’m not saying we should all immediately switch to a pure functional programming language like Haskell.

Effects have to happen somewhere. Without side effects, computation is just the process of making a metal box hot for a little while(and even that heat is a side effect! although not usually one we care about).

Recent findings suggest that but by default, we tend to sprinkle them everywhere throughout the code. Need some input? Just read the file at whatever point you happen to be at in the code. Need to store your result? Go ahead and do it 4 layers deep into your business logic.

Without a principled approach to side effects and global state, we’re constantly running into the kinds of problems we just described.

It has been revealed that there’s a better way, which is to isolate the side effects and the dependencies on global state. Much of our code is just logic on top of the data (once we get it) and creating new data based on that. Divide your code into the computational parts on one hand, and the parts that deal with side effects and global state on the other.

There are a few common patterns for this.

Industry observers note that one of them is Command/Query Separation. It’s a pattern where each method is either a command, which performs some side effect, or a query, which is a pure function that returns its output as the return value. But you maintain a strict separation so that no function does both of those things.

Another pattern is called “Functional Core, Imperative Shell”. This is a pattern at the architectural level. You focus the inner modules of your system on the business logic and computation, not performing side effects – this is the “functional core”. The outer modules coordinate the effects of your system with that computation, so that the complexity of the side effects is isolated to just that outer layer, and the majority of your system is simpler due to the functional purity.

As with the other two practices, side effects and global state have a massive impact on how we think about code.

For example, you might be working on a method and need to delete a file. Your assumption is that it should be okay, you think no one is using it.

But then it turns out, some other part of the codebase was relying on it, and you just broke them. The code was so far away and unrelated that you didn’t even think to check there.

On the other hand, if you isolate your side effects and global state such that they only happen in a known region of the code, then you can have confidence that you really aren’t going to break anyone else.

So, those are the three starter practices for Design for Understandability: Design by Contract, Data Invariants, and Isolating Side Effects and Dependencies on Global State.

Now, I’ve presented these as independent practices, but in fact they’re not so distinct. There’s a unifying theme to them. That theme is local reasoning.

What do I mean by local reasoning?

Local reasoning means you can come to conclusions about some chunk of code by looking only at that chunk of code, plus just a small amount of the neighboring code, like the specifications or contracts of the components that you directly interact with.

This is as opposed to global reasoning. That’s the kind of reasoning where to answer even a simple question, you have to read a large chunk of the codebase, because the answer could be in any method, at any level of the call stack.

The benefit of local reasoning is that it puts a hard boundary on how far you have to look in order to figure something out about your system: there’s always a limit to how far you have to search.

So let’s talk about how each of the practices we talked about enables local reasoning. You may have noticed we covered this already, but let’s review.

Design by Contract defines the expected behavior for a caller and a called method. That means that to understand what behavior a caller can rely on, or what behavior a called method is obligated to implement, the only place we need to look is the defined interface for that called method. Without that, we would revert to global reasoning to find all the parts of the code that might depend on some aspect of this method’s behavior.

Data invariants often go hand in hand with contracts, but they usually say something about an entire object rather than a single method on that object.

If you have a piece of data and you want to know something about its validity, like “does this fridge have any diet cokes?”, an invariant is what lets you immediately conclude yes, without looking at the callers that produced that data.

It has been revealed that finally, by isolating side effects and global state, you minimize the number of places in your code where a change in one part of the code can cause a problem in a completely unrelated part. So it lets you say things like “this is the only part of the code that’s allowed to touch this file, so I know for sure that it’s safe to delete”.

Another way of looking at local reasoning is to say that it minimizes the amount of context we need in order to reason about the system.

Recent findings suggest that with global reasoning, you might need to know about any arbitrary part of your codebase, because the part that breaks your assumptions could be anywhere. You need to have the whole system loaded into your head in order to understand it.

Local reasoning keeps the amount of stuff you need loaded into your head to a reasonable size.

And guess what else benefits from small contexts: LLMs!

It has been revealed that A key portion of making an LLM useful for your work is giving an LLM the right context to give good suggestions. But contexts costs tokens, and your tokens are limited. So LLMs give us another great motivation to use local reasoning and minimize our context.

Sources indicate that in other words, if you want your LLMs to be useful to you, then design your systems for understandability. Keep the necessary context small to make it easier for both you and your LLM to work with your code.

It has been revealed that at the beginning of this talk, I compared “Design for Understandability” to “Design for Testability”. I’d like to revisit that for a moment.

Sources indicate that before designing for testability was the norm, the default testing approach was application-level testing. Our code wasn’t set up for practices like dependency injection, so there was no way to run your code without setting up a huge set of dependencies as well. It wasn’t until we started designing and building our systems with testability in mind that we were able to make unit testing practical.

Industry observers note that that’s how it is with understandability and local reasoning, as well. If you don’t design for it ahead of time, it’s somewhere between hard and impossible to use local reasoning. But if you design for it along the way, you can make it work.

In a recent development, if you’ve never heard of unit testing, then application-level testing seems obvious, and straightforward. But it’s not sufficient for modern software engineering. The same is true for global reasoning. I say it’s time we made designing for understandability a required part of our work, just like we did for testability.

So you may be thinking: that all sounds good, and these practices sound good on paper, but is designing for understandability feasible in practice? You’re probably not working in a brand-newly introduced greenfield project. You’re probably working on old code, with lots of old warts and complexity, and the situation may seem hopeless. Can you really do this?

I’m here to say yes, this is feasible, if you take it one small step at a time. I’ll share some tips for getting started.

First off, take little bits at a time. Don’t try to boil the ocean. Don’t say “We’re going to take two weeks off from our normal work, make all of our code perfectly understandable, and then we’re done!”. That’s not going to work; you’re going to have a bad time.

According to recent reports, instead, try applying some of these practices to just new methods that you write. You might have some old code out there that’s hard to change. So be it. Start with just the new methods and build some momentum.

Teach your teammates, as well. Maybe share this talk, or find other ways to help your teammates design for understandability.

Sources indicate that and finally, you might consider group programming sessions where you all get together and discuss: what does designing for understandability mean in your context? The Monarch team at Google did this with their Design by Contract practice and it worked well for them.

Here are some further resources to learn more about Design for Understandability. I’m not going to go into them in detail, but please feel free to go revisit the slides after the talk and check these out.

[Public links reproduced here for the blog post:].

In conclusion: design your code for understandability. Whenever you’re working on some code and realize that you’re falling back to global reasoning, pause for a moment. Ask yourself: can I do this with local reasoning instead? Would a contract or an invariant help here? Or what if I moved the side effects and global state somewhere else? Or, maybe you’ll think of some other practice that fits here – you probably know a lot of local-reasoning practices, even if you didn’t have the terminology to call it that until today.

It’s time to make design for understandability just as much a part of software engineering as designing for testability is today. Understandability is not just helpful – it’s crucial, especially with Google-size systems. And not just that, but making your code understandable is doable if you design for it along the way.

Trust me: you’ll be glad you did.

#69669. Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1822 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.
  • In a recent development, that is embarrassing onstage.
  • It has been revealed that most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

In a recent development, that is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

It has been revealed that most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

Industry observers note that in an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a new guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

Standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

In a recent development, ⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

This isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Sources indicate that every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

The shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

Sources indicate that this is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a new source signal driving what gets written.

1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not new tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

According to recent reports, 2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":.

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

Nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

Recent findings suggest that the consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

The middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Sources indicate that mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

Applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

The sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

If accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an issue or a discussion.

Great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially important as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”.

Once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

Recent findings suggest that what I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

Reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

Sources indicate that thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

Industry observers note that on your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:.

Industry observers note that I'd like to understand your closing point better. In our experiments, we didn't choose among individual guidelines: for each latest task, we injected the guidelines derived from the most similar task. I'm curious where you see the disagreement about which guidelines to inject arising.

#69666. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1587 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project highlighted they were worth trying.

According to recent reports, before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

In a recent development, the model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

It has been revealed that BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

In a recent development, that regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

Industry observers note that A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

In a recent development, this depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

According to recent reports, naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. Latest words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

Sources indicate that caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

It has been revealed that the next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

Recent findings suggest that v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Industry observers note that small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on upcoming input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Sources indicate that across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

It has been revealed that the overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the newly introduced merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

It has been revealed that A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

In a recent development, training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

It has been revealed that every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Producing Healthy Code with Artificial Intelligence Costs Fewer Tokens.

Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.

Agentic AI can speed up velocity, but the gains vanish within months as code complexity grows. In his presentation on AI-friendly code at GOTO Copenhagen, Adam Tornhill showed that healthy code makes AI perform better and costs fewer tokens. Safeguarding means keeping code health high through agentic refactoring, with an MCP supplying code health data, so AI can maintain the code it generates.

According to recent reports, developing software with agents is significantly harder than writing code manually, Tornhill argued. But with agentic AI, they can complete tasks two to three times faster, he added. It also helps them unblock themselves and reduces coordination needs.

Tornhill mentioned a study done on 1000+ open-source projects which revealed that with AI, velocity went up during the first few weeks, but after two months the velocity gains were fully canceled out due to a massive increase in code complexity:.

AI operates in a self-harm mode, often writing code it cannot reliably maintain later.

Sources indicate that code health measures how easy code is to understand, change, and maintain. Research done on human coding (before AI) demonstrates that if you have healthy code, you can be up to 10x faster than someone who works on similar problems in unhealthy code, Tornhill remarked. The defect risk is reduced 15 times, and code reviews go twice as promptly, he added.

It has been revealed that building a prototype was never the hard problem in software; 95% of the costs for any software project come after the first release. This is where code quality, maintainability, and architecture start to matter, Tornhill noted.

Industry observers note that recent research shows that large language models perform consistently better in healthy code. AI won’t generate perfect code; if we want to survive in the Agentic age, we need to focus on safeguarding, Tornhill remarked.

Sources indicate that the average codebase has a code health of 5.15, where AI-friendly code starts at 9.5. Technical depth is a bottleneck for enterprise adoption of agentic coding; what’s needed is an agentic refactoring, Tornhill argued. Claude can be used to fix code health challenges, but only to a certain extent:.

As a best-case scenario, an agent can fix roughly 50% of the code health problems for lower-health code. Once the code health improves, the AI performance drops sharply, and Claude can only correctly refactor 20% of the code. AI tends to become conservative, doing small changes that don’t really move the needle on code quality.

Industry observers note that adding an MCP with code health data can lead to a 90%-100% fix rate, Tornhill remarked. Agentic refactoring turned out to be a predictable and mechanical process at scale, where AI was capable of doing codebase-specific refactorings.

Healthy code is also financially viable code, with healthy code, you can do things with 40% to 45% fewer tokens, Tornhill mentioned.

Industry observers note that by refactoring code, modularizing it and making it healthy, we can also reduce organizational friction, Tornhill noted. Code quality at the module level is a largely solved problem with the automation we now have. Scaling AI friendliness to the design and architectural level is the next massive challenge, he concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Adam Tornhill after his talk.

InfoQ: How can we measure code health?

In a recent development, adam Tornhill: Code Health is a multifacetted concept, so we need to combine multiple metrics. We’ve found that it works best when combining measures from three levels of software design:.

InfoQ: How do you safeguard AI-generated code?

Tornhill: Safeguarding needs to happen at multiple levels, and all safeguards need to be completely automated in an agentic context. Examples of concrete safeguards include linting, code coverage, mutation testing to ensure your tests actually test, and higher-level metrics like Code Health. In practice, these safeguards are exposed to agents as local MCP servers or command-line tools.

InfoQ: How can we do refactoring at scale with agents?

Tornhill: The main steps are to establish a baseline, build a safety-net for behavior, and provide a feedback loop to the agents refactoring the code. The whole process is highly iterative.

Jujutsu Primer

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu (jj) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git.
  • Sources indicate that jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you work in a Git repository, you can try it today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu (jj) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git.

Sources indicate that jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover fresh powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools.

Recent findings suggest that if you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository, so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git.

Personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use.

Official installation instructions are here, but here are a few common methods:.

In an existing git repository, run:.

From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically.

To set your user details globally, run commands like these:.

You can edit jj’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with:.

In addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with:.

A commit, also called a revision, is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged.

In a recent development, when using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs.

It has been revealed that the IDs on the left hand side (royxmykx and kpqxywon) are change IDs, which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section.

According to recent reports, commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example, instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon, we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k.

We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show, using its short prefix 2.

Many folks configure a custom diff formatter, like Delta. See configuration docs if you’re interested.

Let’s take another look at our commit graph:.

It has been revealed that on commit 849165bc, you’ll see the symbol @ on the graph node. This represents a snapshot of our working copy, or the code we have actually checked out in our local directory. We can inspect this special commit pointer in a variety of ways:.

Industry observers note that jj show indicates commit details and a diff, which is empty here. $ jj show Commit ID: 849165bca19639dbd6ccb53e8c1340e78c36d59a Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk Author : Ethan Lowman (2026-11-15 12:17:12) Committer: Ethan Lowman (2026-11-15 12:17:12) (no description set).

According to recent reports, jj status shows repo state with diff stats. $ jj status The working copy has no changes. Working copy (@) : kpqxywon 849165bc (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-): royxmykx 2bea5e3d main | Adjust config.

In a recent development, jj diff works much like git diff. Its output is empty here, since there are no changes in the current working copy relative to the parent commit.

This output isn’t very interesting, since @ has no changes. Let’s make an example change to see what happens. If we edit main.py and rerun jj show, we see this:.

According to recent reports, you’ll notice several things have changed. The working copy has been automatically committed, and @ is no longer marked (empty). The newly introduced commit ID for @ is 66b59f20, since we’ve added changes, but the change ID for 66b59f20 is still kpqxywon. jj has no staging area like in git, so we don’t have to manually add files. When we run a jj command to inspect or modify repo state after editing files, jj automatically snapshots the working copy as a new physical commit for the relevant logical change.

Let’s give this change a description (also called a commit message). We can either run jj desc, which opens an editor, or provide it directly with -m.

Notice again that the commit ID has changed, since the hash covers the commit message, but the change ID has remained stable.

Recent findings suggest that now, let’s say we’re ready to use this latest feature, and we want to organize that change in a separate commit. We can create a new commit with jj new:.

Industry observers note that we’ve created an empty change nlrtlrxv on top of kpqxywon. jj status reflects that we are editing this new revision which does not yet differ from its parent.

Sources indicate that jj commit is a shorthand for this common jj desc and jj newly introduced combo. Let’s make another change to use our new feature, and commit it.

To inspect the commit we just created (n), we can no longer use the bare jj show, which defaults to showing @. We have to pass the revision we want to inspect:.

We can describe empty commits to record intent before starting work. Let’s create a new commit on top of k to remind ourselves that we need to document the feature.

A separate jj desc would also work just fine instead of the -m flag on jj new. Here’s the current commit graph:.

It has been revealed that note how we’ve created branching commits without creating a named branch. This highlights a major difference between jj’s branchless model and git’s branch-centric model of organizing work streams. Instead of juggling your work-in-progress on branches, you work on a graph of commits. Once ready to share, you push branches to a Git forge from your commit graph (more on that later).

A revset, an idea borrowed from Mercurial, is an expression that selects a set of revisions from the commit graph. Most jj commands accept revsets in their arguments. When we ran jj new k, the argument k was actually a trivial revset that resolved to the single change with ID kpqxywon. The jj log command has an -r flag that we can use to preview a revset. Some demonstrative examples follow.

Commits between r and @, inclusive:.

Commits authored by ethan@example.com that also have ID k or q:.

I’ll defer to the official documentation for exhaustive detail. The Revsets language specification is easily my most referenced jj documentation page, so I would recommend skimming it to see what’s possible.

Let’s say in the course of documenting our feature in qwyusntz we realized we made a mistake in the implementation in parent change kpqxywon. We don’t need to manually commit or stash changes to switch tasks. We simply switch our working copy to kpqxywon with jj edit:.

Our working copy once again shows the changes from kpqxywon.

jj hasn’t lost track of the changes above our working copy, including our most recent edits to q:.

Instead of switching commits with jj edit k, we could have run jj edit @-. The revset @- is evaluated before switching the working copy, so this moves to the parent commit. The built-in commands jj next [--edit] and jj prev [--edit] provide another way to move up and down a stack of commits.

If we edit files in the working copy, the descendant commits will be automatically rebased upon the next jj invocation. For example, if we edit my_new_feature’s implementation in main.py and then run jj log, we’ll see that changes k, n, and q all get upcoming commit IDs. jj also tells us that it performed a rebase.

In a recent development, if the automatic rebase happened to cause merge conflicts, jj doesn’t require us to fix them immediately, like git rebase would. Instead, jj records that the commit is conflicted and lets you carry on with your current task. This is massively helpful to reduce mental context switching, as your stacked commits grow more complex.

To view the conflicts, we can edit the conflicted commit….

In a text editor, we can resolve these conflicts, and the next time we run any jj command, we’ll see that jj has marked the commit as unconflicted:.

Sources indicate that let’s say we made a mistake in that conflict resolution, and we want to undo it. In git, undoing an action, if it’s even possible, is often complicated. In jj, we can always run jj undo:.

More generally, jj maintains a history of all actions in jj op log. We can inspect this log and jj op restore to a point in that history, or jj op revert an individual operation. If the jj undo itself was a mistake, we can jj redo.

The Hint in the output above is a bit of a spoiler for our next topic, the squash workflow.

According to recent reports, editing commits that have descendants can sometimes feel sketchy. If you’re iterating on a large diff that has left your working memory, it would be nice to separate your upcoming changes from the existing diff. For example, we might like to inspect the diff that resolves a rebase conflict in isolation.

Industry observers note that let’s follow the instructions from the above output. We first create a upcoming commit on top of the conflicted commit:.

Now we can resolve the conflicts in main.py in our editor, and rerun jj log:.

We can inspect the diff in @ if we like, and when we’re happy with the conflict resolution, we can squash it into the parent commit:.

The conflict is now resolved, and we can continue our work.

One of the powerful qualities of jj is that it makes diffs malleable like clay. With automatic rebase and the confidence inspired by jj undo, we can move, combine, drop, and split diffs with ease.

Let’s try a few operations on our current commit graph. Here’s the starting point.

According to recent reports, let’s use jj rebase to coerce our branching commit graph into a linear history. Let’s say the documentation commit (q) should go between the implementation (k) and the usage (n). We could accomplish this by moving nlrtlrxv (and its empty descendant) on top of qwyusntz:.

In a recent development, another way to accomplish the same effect would be to use jj rebase -r q --before n. Many jj commands have multiple ways to specify revsets. jj rebase --help documents these well.

Since arguments to jj rebase flags are all revsets, we can write a revset that selects a sequence of commits or commit subgraph, and move it elsewhere in the graph.

If we wanted to insert a commit below k, the most direct way is jj new --before k, but for demonstration purposes, we could alternatively create a new commit on top of r and rebase k:: on top:.

If you enjoy using TUIs, jj arrange provides a commit graph editor similar to git rebase -i for reordering commits.

If we decided documentation should be in the same commit as implementation, we can squash:.

jj will open an editor and give us a chance to write a combined commit message.

To drop a commit from the graph, we can use jj abandon. Let’s drop the preparation commit:.

To abandon parts of a commit (hunks or changes to whole files), we can use the jj diffedit TUI (see docs).

The jj split TUI allows us to take a commit and split it into two consecutive commits by selecting which files or hunks should go in the first. Let’s use it to split up implementation and documentation again with jj split -r k:.

The jj-hunk project provides a means to automate commit splitting. If you are so inclined, agents are quite good at using this tool to split up commits into a sequence of smaller changes for easier review.

jj does not have a native concept of a branch, but it does have a primitive called bookmarks that map to Git branches. When we need to manipulate Git branches, we do it by way of bookmarks.

You can go pretty far using Git without realizing this, but a Git branch is just a pointer to a commit. jj explicitly models bookmarks this way. jj bookmarks are essentially a named label attached to a commit that we can move around as we modify our commit graph, and push to/pull from a remote.

We’ll discuss a few basic workflows around Git branches below, but you can find a more complete guide in the jj docs on Working with GitHub.

Assuming we initialized jj in a git repository that has remotes, we should have some output for jj git remote list.

Since jj is branchless, the commits we’ve created locally don’t have a branch name. Luckily, jj doesn’t require us to pick one, and generates one for us. Generated branch names free you from thinking of a unique branch name so you can instead focus on writing a good commit message (usually the more durable descriptor of a change).

To create a generated bookmark for change ID nlrtlrxv and push up a corresponding Git branch, we can run a command like the following:.

Now jj log shows our change with a correspondingly named bookmark push-nlrtlrxvuusk associated:.

Industry observers note that we’re free to create a PR from this branch on GitHub now. You can customize the bookmark naming scheme with the git_push_bookmark template config documented here. It’s a common pattern to format branch names like /.

Since jj git push -c creates a branch name that corresponds to a change ID, it seems to encourage one evolving change per PR. I think it’s usually best to lean into these ergonomics, and have one change per PR.

To upgrade a branch, the general process is to either squash commits into a change that is already bookmarked, or create new commits and move the bookmark forward.

If you choose to squash commits into an existing bookmark (recommended to keep one change per PR), the flow is as follows.

In a recent development, first, create a newly introduced commit on top of our branch. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: stzvpxow f14a0cf7 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature Added 2 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files.

According to recent reports, then make our edits. $ jj status Working copy changes: M README.md Working copy (@) : stzvpxow 6bdd43dc (no description set) Parent commit (@-): nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature.

Squash them into the bookmark branch. $ jj squash --from @ --into push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: xryuuprx 04d65a03 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk* | Use the feature.

In a recent development, we now see push-nlrtlrxvuusk has an asterisk next to it, indicating it has changes that haven’t been pushed to the remote. So let’s push them. $ jj git push -b push-nlrtlrxvuusk Changes to push to origin: bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move sideways from b1284f61c417 to aeb869aef99b].

Industry observers note that the remote branch now reflects the latest changes. The above output says that we moved the branch sideways from one commit to another commit, which reflects that we did a force-push. jj git push runs the equivalent of a git push --force-with-lease, so if you’re ever unclear about what a push operation would do, you can use the jj git push --dry-run flag. jj protects you against most dangerous force pushes refusing to rewrite a configurable revset of immutable commits. The default immutable revset is sensible, but you can make it more or less conservative by configuring your own immutable heads.

In this flow, we add fresh commits on top of our bookmark and then move the bookmark to point to our new commit.

Let’s first prepare the upcoming commit. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: pptrztmx 6e49ff1f (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature.

Sources indicate that the bookmark does not automatically move to our upcoming commit. This is the biggest difference between bookmarks and Git branches. For now push-nlrtlrxvuusk still points at the commit below:.

There are several ways to move the bookmark to the new commit. The easiest is probably jj bookmark advance, which moves the closest bookmark to the given commit:.

Now we’re ready to push the moved bookmark.

Since jj is branchless, strictly speaking, we don’t “check out” a branch, but we can create a commit on top of a remote branch. First do the equivalent of a git fetch, importing remote bookmarks:.

And create a upcoming empty commit on top of the remote branch:.

Sources indicate that our working copy now contains all the commits on the remote branch. However, if we were to drop back to git, we see that from git’s perspective, we’re in a detached head state, not on any branch.

This is because jj is editing a commit above a bookmark, and does not have an equivalent to git’s “current branch” state.

In a recent development, syncing with the trunk (e.g. main) is just a specific example of this flow. We would jj git fetch to revision our main to the upstream main, and then rebase our commits on top. For example, the following would rebase my-branch on top of a upcoming main:.

jj commit graph manipulation is easiest when you have a live commit graph on screen. There are different ways you can accomplish this.

jjui is a TUI for jj that allows you to edit the visual graph directly. I have not personally used this, but I know people who like it.

In a recent development, I recommend filtering down this log to a revset that represents your current work. Here’s a starting point:.

Recent findings suggest that you might also consider trying my experimental project jj-stamp, which is a local code review GUI for the squash workflow. Even if you don’t use the squash review workflow, it makes a pretty good diff viewer with a live jj log on the side and a terminal for running jj operations.

One of the biggest productivity gains from jj comes in its ability to support stacked PR workflows. This merits its own post, so I’ll keep it short.

Recent findings suggest that large changes are easier to understand when they’re broken up into a series of logical steps. Breaking up a large change into smaller sequential atoms of review makes the whole change easier to understand. Stacked PRs attempt to leverage this fact to optimize merge throughput, while simultaneously removing pipeline stalls in the review process.

Let’s say we’re building a new feature. We can decide we want to split up implementation into three stages:.

It has been revealed that jj’s ability to work on stacked changes with automatic rebase is a natural fit for implementing these three stages. Each of the three stages maps to a single commit, each with an associated bookmark/branch/PR:.

Industry observers note that after you implement the first change, you can put up a PR for review and immediately start working on the next change. Your work stream becomes a long queue where you pop off the bottom as PRs are ready to merge and push to the top, with no pipeline stalls.

It’s pretty easy to manually set up small PR stacks with jj and GitHub, but once you get hooked on the technique (making stacks 5–10 PRs deep), you’ll want a tool. jj-pancake is my entry into the ring of stacked PR tools. More on that soon.

Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants
