💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs.
  • Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that.
  • And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

Recent findings suggest that GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so people can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

Sources indicate that we want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

Recent findings suggest that GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

Recent findings suggest that for models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

Industry observers note that the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

It has been revealed that when GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

In a recent development, llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for latest architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

It has been revealed that that opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

According to recent reports, our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

According to recent reports, the kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

In a recent development, to show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Sources indicate that faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

According to recent reports, the initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an glitch with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful...
  • The manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads:.

I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful...

...until recently (October 2026):.

This is un-fucking-acceptable. As in, absolutely fucking not.

The manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit.

ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit.

The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally.

Sources indicate that these were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here.

The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need.

My router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. Apple's HomeKit just worked and I'm able to control them with voice commands: “Hey Siri, open Door 1”.

When I was growing up, my father wired a mercury switch onto our garage door that lit up a light in the hallway when we'd left the garage door open. This was a valuable signal that helped our family avoid accidentally leaving the door open overnight. Since the ratgdo32 has a JSON status endpoint, I was able to rebuild Dad's solution in software with Slack:.

The script runs at night checking for an open door:.

The repo maintainer made my day when I submitted a tiny pull request: "Simple and useful. Happy to merge this. Thank you.".

It has been revealed that both boards are now reachable over my Tailscale network, so my monitoring software can load /healthcheck. This required a custom route:.

After approving the route, my monitoring software can verify the hardware is working.

Everything runs locally with no cloud, and notifications now say who opened the door which myQ never did.

To anyone at Chamberlain responsible for myQ, I offer my sincerest Fuck You.

Miro vs. Notion: Which Is Better for Team Collaboration?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review.
  • It has been revealed that A team can leave a workshop with a wall full of ideas and still have no usable record of what it decided.
  • Both feature in our best AI collaboration tools guide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review. This does not influence our editorial evaluations. Read our affiliate disclosure.

It has been revealed that A team can leave a workshop with a wall full of ideas and still have no usable record of what it decided. Miro and Notion help at different points in that journey. Miro is our choice for visual thinking and facilitated collaboration. Notion is our recommendation for keeping decisions, documents, and ongoing intends useful after the meeting.

Both feature in our best AI collaboration tools guide. The notable choice is whether your team needs a shared canvas to develop its thinking or a structured workspace to preserve and use it.

In a recent development, miro gives a group a shared surface on which to make a problem visible. A customer journey can sit beside research notes, a process map, and competing proposals. The arrangement matters: colleagues can see relationships that would be harder to follow across separate documents. That makes Miro especially useful before the answer is settled.

In a recent development, its diagramming tools support flowcharts and technical diagrams, while presentation and facilitation features help a group work through material together. Miro also includes Docs, Tables, timelines, and Kanban formats on the canvas. It can carry a workshop into a initiative without requiring every result to be exported immediately.

Official Miro guide to using its AI canvas.

We recommend Miro for product discovery, design workshops, process improvement, and technical discussions where seeing the system helps people understand it. The tradeoff is the freedom of the canvas. A sprawling board needs clear frames, ownership, and a useful conclusion; otherwise colleagues return to a large collection of objects without knowing where to start.

Industry observers note that notion starts with a page rather than a canvas. That page can hold a proposal, a decision, an onboarding guide, or a database view showing the tasks connected to it. The result suits work that people need to read, upgrade, and find again. A well-maintained product brief stays useful long after the discussion that created it.

Recent findings suggest that the strength is the connection between explanation and structure. A research database can link to a roadmap; a roadmap item can link to its specification and meeting notes. Notion’s wiki tools add a stronger home for shared knowledge, including page ownership and verification. Its project features also include subtasks, dependencies, and timelines.

Official Notion introduction to projects and tasks.

We prefer Notion for a company handbook, an editorial operation, or a product team that wants its reasoning beside its initiative. Someone still needs to maintain the organization. Its flexible pages work best when there is an agreed home for vital information and a clear owner for keeping it reliable.

Industry observers note that consider a product team trying to improve its first-week customer experience. It has interview notes, a rough journey map, several proposed changes, and a deadline for choosing what to build. Here is how we would use each tool for the same project.

Sources indicate that our choice: Miro. Arrange the customer journey, interview observations, and friction points on one board. Keep the original notes beside the proposed themes so colleagues can inspect the evidence behind a suggestion. This is a stronger working surface when the group needs to move ideas around, spot relationships, and compare alternatives together.

In a recent development, in Notion, we would organize the interview notes in a research database and write a synthesis page. That is a good fit for an asynchronous review, especially when colleagues primarily need to read the findings rather than rearrange them in a workshop.

In a recent development, our choice: Notion. Give the agreed change a brief containing the customer problem, selected approach, evidence, and owner. Link it to tasks with a status and deadline. A latest collaborator should be able to understand both what the team chose and why it chose it.

According to recent reports, miro can also keep the plan on its canvas using Docs, Tables, and timelines. We would stay there when the map remains the team’s main working surface. We would prefer Notion when the result becomes an ongoing specification, operating guide, or searchable record that colleagues maintain between meetings.

Sources indicate that if the team uses both products, put the exploration in Miro and the approved brief in Notion. Link the board from the brief, name the decision owner, and agree which task list is authoritative. The benefit comes from preserving the thinking without maintaining two competing versions of the delivery strategy.

In a recent development, for a service-design workshop, a visual map lets participants place observations beside the stage of the customer experience they describe. They can group related problems, trace dependencies, and vote on priorities. Miro’s Starter initiative includes a timer, voting, and private mode, which are useful tools for running that session rather than merely recording its notes.

Recent findings suggest that notion is better suited to the brief before the session and the agreed decisions afterward. It can host collaborative notes and embed supporting material, but we would choose Miro when the exercise depends on arranging, connecting, and discussing objects across an open surface.

Recent findings suggest that A workshop output becomes more valuable when it has an owner, a next action, and a dependable home. Notion makes that transition natural: a decision can become a page with context, linked tasks, and a place for later revisions. Database views help people see the part of the plan relevant to them.

Miro’s Tables and Docs make it a more capable ongoing workspace than a simple whiteboard. We would keep a visually complex roadmap there when the surrounding maps remain essential. For policies, research libraries, and specifications that colleagues primarily read and search, Notion is our clearer recommendation.

In a recent development, miro’s Create with AI tools can use selected board content to generate output, turn sticky notes into a document, and group notes by keyword or sentiment. This is useful after a workshop: a facilitator can turn a crowded board into an initial summary while preserving the visual material that produced it.

That context has boundaries. Miro’s AI overview explains that canvas-visible material is central to its processing. An embedded tool does not automatically give the assistant unrestricted access to everything behind it. Miro AI also uses credits, with consumption depending on the feature.

Industry observers note that notion AI is the better fit when the useful context lives in pages and databases. Its agent can help create and edit that workspace, while search and meeting notes support finding information and capturing discussion. We recommend Miro for synthesizing visual discovery and Notion for producing work from maintained team knowledge.

Recent findings suggest that in Miro, we would select the onboarding observations and ask for a summary of the main friction points, with related notes grouped into themes. The useful result is a clearer discussion surface: the facilitator can see which observations support each theme and whether an notable exception has been lost in the grouping.

In a recent development, in Notion, the next request would be: “Draft an onboarding improvement brief using these research pages, link the evidence, and organize the agreed actions in our task database.” Its agent can create and edit pages and databases within the user’s access. That is the more useful direction when the output should become maintained documentation and structured follow-through.

In a recent development, our preference is Miro for making sense of workshop material and Notion for turning maintained knowledge into a reusable work product. Neither output establishes that a proposed improvement will help customers; the team still owns the decision and the implementation.

Recent findings suggest that these are USD monthly equivalents with annual billing from Miro’s pricing page and Notion’s pricing page. Miro Free allows three editable boards; Starter adds unlimited private boards. Business adds signed-in guest collaboration and more advanced planning and visual features.

It has been revealed that notion Free is useful for personal organization, but collaborative blocks are limited for workspaces with two or more members. Plus expands the shared workspace; Business is the more relevant tier for the included AI capabilities discussed here. Notion’s AI allowance rules distinguish Standard and Select usage, with optional additional workspace credits. An AI-enabled subscription does not mean every type of usage is unlimited.

Recent findings suggest that miro earns its subscription when better workshops and clearer maps improve decisions. Notion earns it when it becomes the place colleagues reliably find the context they need. Buying both can be sensible for a discovery-heavy product team, provided the final decision and its owner have one agreed home.

In a recent development, for ten paid members on annual billing, Miro Starter is $960 a year at $8 per member per month. Notion Plus is $1,200 a year at $10. These are useful entry paid plans, but they do not include the same capabilities.

How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.
  • As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly vital sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly vital sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

Industry observers note that this builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Industry observers note that transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

In a recent development, these results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Industry observers note that reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News .NET 11 : ASP.NET Core: Union Type Support, OpenAPI 3.2 by Default and Blazor AI Components.

Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.

Last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release. The patch spans Minimal APIs, OpenAPI, SignalR, Blazor, authentication, and the Kestrel server. As stated in the announcement, .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support.

In a recent development, on the API side, developers can now use C# 15 union types in JSON request and response bodies across Minimal APIs and MVC. The release notes limit the feature to JSON bodies, so route, query, header, and form values cannot bind to a union.

Minimal API validation also runs asynchronous validators, which keeps threads free while a rule waits on a database lookup or a remote call. The framework can now localize validation messages and display names itself, and endpoints can skip the remaining middleware pipeline through a new [ShortCircuit] attribute.

Developers who generate OpenAPI documents now get version 3.2 unless they select an earlier one for tooling that has not caught up. As described in the release notes, the framework depends on Microsoft.OpenApi 3.3.1 for this, and the notes label that update a breaking change.

Sources indicate that with 3.2, endpoints that stream server-sent events are documented with a schema for each event's payload, and the generator emits an anyOf schema for unions. Generated documents can also describe endpoints that use the HTTP QUERY method, and APIs that carry the [Obsolete] attribute show up as deprecated.

In a recent development, signalR adds authentication refresh, so a long-lived connection no longer has to close when its access token expires. As reported, server developers enable it per hub, while the .NET client refreshes automatically by default and the TypeScript client can do the same. Blazor passes the refreshed identity on to Interactive Server components while the circuit stays connected.

Blazor receives the longest list of changes, and many of them target static server-side rendering. With the latest CacheView component, developers can cache the rendered markup of a component subtree, and the child components do not run when a cached copy is served. Blazor now ships client-side validation for static SSR forms, enabled by default.

Developers can also carry data between requests with TempData or session values. According to the release notes, the Blazor Web App template drops its app.UseAntiforgery() call, because a middleware for CSRF protection is now added by default.

For Interactive Server apps, an opt-in package pauses the circuit of a hidden browser tab after a delay, two minutes by default, to free server memory. Lists built with Virtualize may now mix items of different heights, and Microsoft raised the default OverscanCount from 3 to 15. Page and sort state in QuickGrid now lives in the URL query string, with sortable headers and pager controls rendered as links instead of buttons.

It has been revealed that the release notes flag this as a CSS breaking change, because custom styles written for the buttons also have to target the links. The release also includes Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI, a set of components for chat and agent interfaces. According to the announcement, Microsoft treats that package as experimental and will keep it in prerelease throughout .NET 11.

On the security and server side, an experimental package adds Device Bound Session Credentials, a protocol that ties session refresh to a private key held by the browser. Response compression and request decompression gain Zstandard support, which is on by default.

Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 parser no longer throws exceptions on malformed requests, a change that is reported to raise throughput by up to 20 to 40 percent under heavy invalid traffic. The shared framework libraries of ASP.NET Core are now compiled with runtime-async, described in the release notes as an internal change with no public API impact.

According to recent reports, two older APIs are on the way out. The Microsoft.AspNetCore.Grpc.Swagger package is now deprecated, and Kestrel's TlsClientHelloBytesCallback option is obsolete in favor of the new UseTlsClientHelloListener extension.

Other changes in this release are native OpenTelemetry tracing attributes, client-side cancellation of SignalR hub invocations, scrolling to a specific item in Virtualize and QuickGrid, passkey display names inferred from the authenticator, and TimeProvider support in ASP.NET Core Identity.

For interested readers and developers, the full release notes are available in the What's newly introduced in ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 article on Microsoft Learn.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for media inquiries, call CWA Communications at 202-434-1168 or email comms@cwa-union.org. To read about CWA Members, Leadership or Industries, visit our About page.

San Francisco, Calif. — On Friday, November 20, workers at Internet Archive announced their intent to form a union with the Communications Workers of America (CWA). They are seeking to join CWA Local 9415 in Oakland, California.

Sources indicate that in a letter sent this morning via email, members of the union’s organizing committee presented management with a request for voluntary recognition after a supermajority of eligible workers signed cards signaling their desires for union representation. Worker-organizers for the union have also simultaneously filed a petition for a union certification election with the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB); if Internet Archive grants the union’s request for voluntary recognition, organizers will withdraw the NLRB petition.

It has been revealed that “We are forming a union because we care deeply about the Internet Archive, its patrons, and its place as a vital part of the internet ecosystem. Now more than ever, we want the Internet Archive to last for the generations to come,” said organizing committee member Danielle Leard, a digitization technician for the Internet Archive. “Sustaining workers long-term, through job security, livable wages, and sufficient benefits, goes hand-in-hand with sustaining the Archive long-term.”.

It has been revealed that “Throughout the years, many of us have witnessed the significant extent to which the Internet Archive and its patrons benefit from some of the most talented, dedicated, and overall purpose-driven folks that we’ve had the privilege of working alongside,” stated organizing committee member Chelsea Richelle Smith, a patron services specialist at Internet Archive. “At its core, we all share the collective desire to foster a workplace in which everyone thrives. We believe in continuing to build towards a democratic environment where the workers have a meaningful voice in the work that we do and the conditions under which that work is done, in alignment with each other and the organization’s overall mission.”.

It has been revealed that the Internet Archive is one of the world’s largest and oldest libraries of digitized media, with nearly 120 librarians, engineers, technicians, project managers, media specialists, facilities workers, and administrative staff making up the proposed unit. Together, Internet Archive workers ensure that the Archive remains a beacon of equitable knowledge to millions of consumers worldwide through several different services, such as the Wayback Machine, Open Library, and most recently, the digital preservation of government documents.

“In solidarity with workers across the country, we aim to model the practice of workplace democracy and the building of technology that benefits the public,” said organizing committee member Will Howes, an engineer on the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine. “We organized the Internet Archive not only for each other as coworkers, but to show the tech and non-profit sectors what is possible. Any worker can and should believe that talking to their colleagues today is the first step towards improving their workplace conditions.”.

The union’s announcement marks the latest effort to democratize universal and free access to knowledge; in September, U.S.-based Wikimedia Foundation workers secured union recognition with CWA, and in the union’s vision statement, worker organizers cited the successful unionization efforts at the Free Software Foundation (FSF) and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) as inspirations for organizing.

“In a rapidly evolving technology landscape, collective action and strong workplace protections help ensure that workers are heard and respected,” mentioned CWA Local 9415 President Decovan Rhem. “We are proud to stand strong with the Internet Archive workers to obtain union recognition and advocate for a positive, inclusive workplace.”.

The union has introduced a petition to garner public support for voluntary recognition. For more updates, follow Internet Archive Labor Union-CWA Local 9415 (IALU-CWA) on Bluesky, Instagram, Mastodon, and Tumblr.

The Campaign to Organize Digital Employees (CODE-CWA) is a network of worker-organizers and their staff working every single day to build the voice and power necessary to ensure the future of the tech, game, and digital industries in the United States and Canada. CODE-CWA is a project of the Communications Workers of America, which represents hundreds of thousands of workers throughout tech, media, telecom, and other industries who stand together to fight for justice on the job and in our communities.

Industry observers note that the BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

  • In a recent development, enterprise customers were carved out.
  • When your data sits on someone else’s platform, someone else’s legal fights, contracts and policies decide what happens to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that that meant chats consumers had already asked to delete. It covered ChatGPT Free, Plus, Pro and Team accounts, plus API customers without a zero-data-retention agreement. OpenAI fought it. Its COO, Brad Lightcap, called it “an overreach.” The broad order ended in late September, but data from accounts the Times flagged stays on legal hold.

In a recent development, enterprise customers were carved out. Plenty of business teams on Team prepares and standard API keys were not. None of them were parties to the case. They hit delete. A judge in someone else’s lawsuit decided delete didn’t mean delete.

I’m not picking on OpenAI. They pushed back hard. That’s the point. When your data sits on someone else’s platform, someone else’s legal fights, contracts and policies decide what happens to it.

According to recent reports, now swap in your own organization. Your contracts, your claims files, your source code, your customers’ health records. More and more of it is flowing through AI models running on infrastructure you don’t own, governed by terms you didn’t write.

That’s what sovereign AI is really about. Not flags and borders. Control.

McKinsey surveyed 300 executives, investors and government officials late last year. Seventy-one percent called sovereign AI an “existential concern” or a “strategic imperative.” McKinsey sizes it as a $600 billion market by 2030, with up to 40% of AI workloads potentially moving into sovereign environments.

In a recent development, notice the thread. Sovereignty and open source keep showing up together. That’s not an accident.

In a recent development, I’ve said it before: the models are good enough. For most of the day-to-day work enterprises actually need, summarization, research, instruction following, document processing, the frontier gains don’t move the needle. A model that wins an Olympiad math contest doesn’t make your claims process any faster.

I’ve run open models like Qwen on my own hardware and watched them handle real application tasks well. I can fine-tune on my own data, on my own machine, without sending a single record out the door. Two years ago that wasn’t a serious enterprise option. Today it is.

In a recent development, that changes the sovereignty math. You don’t have to build a frontier model to own your AI. You can take a strong open-weight model, run it inside your own walls or a sovereign cloud, tune it on your data and keep the weights.

The supply side is moving too. In August, Nvidia agreed to pay Poolside $6 billion to license its model-building platform and offered jobs to more than 100 of its engineers, all aimed at its Nemotron family of open-weight models. When the firm that sells the picks and shovels pours that kind of money into open models, the open models are going to keep getting better.

It has been revealed that and the security tooling is catching up. Confidential inference uses a trusted execution environment inside the CPU or GPU so data stays encrypted until it reaches a walled-off section of the chip. Even the cloud provider can’t see it. That moves you from hoping your data is safe to knowing it is.

So yes. Sovereign AI can be really, really good. Lower cost per workload, no surprise price hikes, no model deprecated out from under you, and a straight answer when your board asks where the data goes.

But I’d be doing you a disservice if I stopped there.

Compute is concentrated, and it isn’t cheap. The Center for a New American Security’s Sovereign AI Index finds about 90% of frontier AI compute sits in the United States and China. McKinsey notes only about 30 countries host compute capable of advanced AI workloads. Owning your stack means GPUs, power, cooling and people who know how to run them. Budget for all of it, not just the chips.

Sovereign doesn’t mean self-sufficient. CNAS tracks 184 government-backed sovereign AI projects. More than three-fifths disclose at least one foreign partner, and most of those partners are U.S. companies. Even nations can’t do this alone. The World Economic Forum and Bain argue sovereignty is really “strategic interdependence.” I agree. Decide which layers you must control and which you can safely rent.

Open models still trail on the hardest tasks. McKinsey flags that localized models can fall short of frontier performance. For some workloads that gap matters. The answer isn’t all or nothing. Route sensitive, high-volume work to models you own, and keep a governed path to frontier APIs for the problems that truly need them.

Industry observers note that operations is where most programs break. Infrastructure, data and model control get the attention. Operational sovereignty, who can access the system, who can change its configuration, who can audit what it did, is the pillar most enterprises miss. That gets serious fast once AI agents start taking actions on your behalf. If an outside vendor holds the keys to your agents, you don’t have sovereign AI. You have a hosted service with a nicer name.

Don’t lock yourself in a fresh box. The point of sovereignty is choice. Build so you can swap models without rebuilding everything around them. If your “sovereign” stack only runs one model from one vendor, you’ve just moved the dependency.

Recent findings suggest that the organizations getting this right treat each piece as an engineering requirement with an owner and a metric. Where does inference physically happen? Where are prompts and outputs logged, and for how long? Which model sees which data? Who can turn it off?

The ones struggling treat sovereign AI as a checkbox on a vendor questionnaire.

It has been revealed that this is consistent with everything I see in our work at Marlabs. The model is rarely the problem anymore. The implementation is. The humans, the architecture, the governance. Sovereign AI doesn’t change that. It raises the stakes on getting it right.

It has been revealed that those Team-plan users didn’t do anything wrong. They trusted their vendor agreement. The decision about their data got made in a courtroom they never entered.

It has been revealed that you get to make that decision yourself. When your board, your regulator or your biggest customer asks who controls their data and who else can see it, sovereign AI done well gives you a straight answer. Point to exactly where it lives. Show them who has the keys.

In a recent development, that’s worth building. Just build it with your eyes open.

Industry observers note that what’s driving the sovereign AI conversation in your organization? Let me know.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reinforcement Learning environments give latest capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • In a recent development, an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that indicates up in the new RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reinforcement Learning environments give latest capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

In a recent development, an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that indicates up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Recent findings suggest that every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, consumers of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

According to recent reports, we think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

It has been revealed that the frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

Recent findings suggest that the dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

In a recent development, the RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Industry observers note that framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

In a recent development, here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

Recent findings suggest that the command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

It has been revealed that A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

It has been revealed that that is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

Industry observers note that we opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

Sources indicate that the first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your owners publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 21, 2026 in release.

Announcing the release of Alice v0.6.0!

This change introduces several new features needed to build a small collection of packages from the Opam repository which I’ve been manually porting to Alice’s package format in alice-ports.

According to recent reports, alice packages may now refer to modules from the standard library which are excluded from the prelude, such as Unix and Str. A new builtins section in Alice.kdl can be used to list the built-in modules a package can access:.

Industry observers note that packages may include C source files in their src directory. All C files will be compiled and linked into the resulting executable when building a project. The ability to compile C code raises the question of how to pass custom linker arguments to the C compiler, and this is addressed with another new feature: config scripts.

According to recent reports, A package may include a config script in a file named config.ml file in the package’s root directory (next to Alice.kdl). The config.ml file is compiled and executed as the first step of building a package, and any lines in its standard output beginning with alice: are interpreted by Alice as directives that can influence the build. Currently the only supported directives are alice:print_endline which prints a message, and alice:add_c_linker_args which adds C linker arguments.

Recent findings suggest that config scripts can depend on other packages, and also access built-in modules from the standard library. This can be configured in Alice.kdl:.

Sources indicate that config scripts are expected to be run only once each time they are compiled because their output can be trivially cached in the build directory. For this reason it’s faster to compile config scripts with the bytecode compiler rather than the native compiler, and of course this means compiling all their dependencies with the bytecode compiler too.

This was a necessary feature for allowing config scripts to be built with the bytecode compiler, but it might also be something people find useful to integrate into their workflow, since the bytecode compiler backend is generally faster than the native backend (but of course the executables it produces are generally slower to run).

Sources indicate that commands that compile code (e.g. alice build, alice run) now take a --backend argument which can be passed native or bytecode. The default is native.

On Windows, Alice v0.6.0 can be installed with WinGet:.

On macOS and Linux, the latest version of Alice can be installed with Homebrew:.

Alternatively, on macOS and Linux, Alice v0.6.0 can be installed by running the install script:.

On NixOS, Alice v0.6.0 can be installed via the flake github:alicecaml/alice#alice_0_6_0.default, e.g.:.

Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that holo4 is our latest series of agentic models.
  • In a recent development, holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • Sources indicate that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that holo4 is our latest series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

In a recent development, holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Sources indicate that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

Sources indicate that OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

It has been revealed that automationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Sources indicate that build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

According to recent reports, the tower is square in blueprint at every height, never round. InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer.

Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Jordan Cutler, Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest, presented how the role of a staff engineer changes when every engineer has access to the same AI tools. The session argued that most "AI for engineers" content focuses on individual productivity, while the real question for staff engineers is where their leverage comes from now. According to Cutler, AI did not change what a staff engineer is for, but it changed where the leverage is.

The talk opened with a reflection on Cutler's previous conference talk, where he showed how AI could turn a four-hour task into four minutes. At that point he was shipping roughly as much as his whole team, which he described as multiplying himself rather than his team. That framed the central question of the session: what does a 10x engineer look like when everyone has AI?

In a recent development, to illustrate why this matters, Cutler shared internal Pinterest data on merged pull requests per engineer per week between Q1 2025 and Q3 2026. The top 10% of engineers went from 6.7 to 11.3 merged PRs per week, a 68% increase, while the bottom half went from 1.0 to 1.15, an increase of 14%. Everyone has AI, but not everyone uses it the same way, and the gap keeps growing. The presentation organized the response to that gap into three moves: multiply yourself, multiply your team, and multiply the system.

It has been revealed that the first move, multiply yourself, is about going first. Cutler explained that he tries fresh tools before his team does, and that part of that work is hitting dead ends so others don't have to. He mentioned examples such as an agent harness that could not be steered mid-task and a remote agent runner that required too many follow-ups. Sharing those findings early means the team does not lose a week on the same experiments. Running many agents also revealed a new problem: he kept giving the same corrections in every session, such as avoiding em-dashes, adding a diagram to the PR description, and keeping pull requests small.

The second move, multiply your team, started from a limitation: the folder made him faster, but only he had it. With new people joining the team and a new area to ramp up on, Cutler found himself repeating the same comments in code review, such as asking why a value is null instead of fixing the cause, testing like a user would, and keeping PRs small. The talk emphasized that the value of encoding that judgment grows with every teammate who adopts it, compared to the flat curve of a single engineer working alone.

It has been revealed that the third move, multiply the system, is about moving up a level. Cutler used the history of container shipping as an analogy: ports got better at loading cargo by hand, but the standard box changed the economics entirely, from $5.86 a ton to 16 cents a ton. At Pinterest, migrations were the cargo, one kind of change spread across hundreds of files and dozens of teams. Instead of running each migration by hand, the team built a system where a staff engineer points to a initiative and an example, an engineer puts it on a schedule, and an agent running in a sandbox splits the work into PRs team by team. A class component migration ran three to five times faster than by hand, in the background while teams worked on other things.

Industry observers note that the talk also covered what went wrong. One scheduled job looped and opened 16 PRs in two minutes, increasing CI wait times from under 30 seconds to 14 minutes. The lesson was not to wait for the perfect guardrail, but to ship a small one. Cutler encouraged attendees to find their own "any" problem: a first responder for any incident, a draft fix for any bug ticket, or an agent that triages any flaky test. Today, 40 engineers have scheduler jobs of their own.

The results were significant. Using the same AI tools as other web teams, Cutler's team now ships about four times as much per engineer, without counting his own PRs.

Industry observers note that the presentation concluded with practical steps: write down what you repeat, put it where people already work, and build for every case instead of one. Some parts of the job cannot be written down, like an honest conversation with a teammate who is struggling, and those remain the staff engineer's responsibility. As Cutler put it, a 10x engineer isn't ten times faster, they are the reason ten other people are. As AI agents become part of everyday development workflows, the role of senior engineers may increasingly shift from personal output toward encoding judgment into the tools, defaults, and systems that entire organizations use.

#69640. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1849 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Sources indicate that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • In a recent development, consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this initiative includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Sources indicate that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

In a recent development, consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this initiative includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern demonstrates up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

Industry observers note that A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

Sources indicate that this is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

It has been revealed that provenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

Sources indicate that we tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts remarked 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

In a recent development, binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a recent development, in a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an key area for improvement.

It has been revealed that we also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This highlights it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

It has been revealed that blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

Industry observers note that that adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

It has been revealed that want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

In a recent development, source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Recent findings suggest that practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval states "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the problem well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

Recent findings suggest that I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Industry observers note that like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

According to recent reports, however, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce upcoming errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.
