📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brad Wardell is Founder and CEO of Clairvoyance AI and the founder and CEO of Stardock. He has spent more than three decades building desktop software and strategy games, including products such as Fences and Galactic Civilizations. His work on game development pipelines, creative assets, and everyday business reporting shaped his interest in persistent AI agents that can work directly with local files and applications.

According to recent reports, clairvoyance AI develops a workspace for named AI staff with ongoing assignments and memory, connecting local files and development tools with cloud services and models running on a user’s own hardware. Incubated at Stardock, it supports workflows that produce reusable notes, reports, and other artifacts. In this interview, Wardell discusses how game development informed the product, where local models fit into daily work, and the routing, memory, and permission controls needed to make agents useful.

In a recent development, you’ve spent more than three decades building desktop software and strategy games at Stardock, including products such as Fences and Galactic Civilizations. What problem inside your own business prompted you to build Clairvoyance AI, and when did you realize it could become a firm of its own?

The real pressure point was Ara: History Untold, which Stardock helped Microsoft and Oxide Games finish. A huge amount of time was going into just moving creative assets into the game. Writing came in as .DOCX files that had to be painstakingly hand-converted into XML or CSV. 3D assets had to be carefully brought into our engine. A single balance change meant touching a dozen different files. Localization meant matching translated strings back to the right keys in the right files by hand. Clairvoyance AI made all of that painless and let us ship on time.

By late 2025, we had an internal debate about whether to make it public at all. It was a real competitive advantage, like having a superset of something like OpenClaw a year early. What pushed us toward going public was watching friends and colleagues lose jobs to AI automation that they could have kept if they’d had better tools. At that point, we knew we wanted to open Clairvoyance AI to the public.

Sources indicate that you’ve argued that many AI agent tools reveal a lack of experience shipping consumer software. What mistakes do you see most often, and what lessons from your own career should AI developers be applying?

Sources indicate that the biggest tell is terminology. If you don’t already know the words, like “glyph” for the little graphic on a button, you’re at a real disadvantage talking to an AI, because it’s trained on people who already know the lingo. Most of the teams building these tools are very smart but very young, and it demonstrates in the usability choices. A good example is when Anthropic added the ability to drag text from one terminal session to another, that got millions of views. We’ve had agents that you can just @ by name to hand off work automatically, no dragging anything. Theirs requires the user to do the work the AI should be doing.

The lesson from 30 years of shipping desktop software is that you have to actually use the thing you’re building, every day, with real deadlines, before anyone outside the tech giant sees it. A lot of AI products feel like they were built by people who haven’t had to live inside their own software.

According to recent reports, you describe the next phase of AI as a routing problem: deciding what runs on a device, across a local network, or in the cloud. Could you walk us through a real workflow and explain how those decisions should be made?

In a recent development, routing isn’t really an individual decision anymore, it’s becoming a company-level one. We’re about to release a feature called Hivemind that makes this concrete. Most enterprises already own plenty of capable machines that sit idle every night. Hivemind lets a company pool those idle GPUs across its own machines so anyone on the team can run AI work on them instead of sending it to the cloud. If you’re tracking tens of thousands of shipments across a supply chain, or auditing where a company’s money went, you don’t need a frontier cloud model for that. You need enough compute, and most companies already have it sitting unused after hours.

Industry observers note that at the individual level, the same logic applies, just on a smaller scale. I run dashboards, crash reports, sentiment reports, and sales data every night on a local model instead of a cloud one. I used to run that same workload through Claude and it cost about $100 a month in tokens. Now it runs for free overnight on hardware I already own, and I read the results in the morning.

So the actual decision isn’t “local versus cloud,” it’s “does this need to happen while someone is staring at the screen, and does the company already have the hardware to do it without paying per-token.”.

You believe a substantial share of everyday agentic work can already run on local hardware. Which tasks have you demonstrated this with, on what hardware, and how do you measure success beyond whether a model produces a plausible answer?

We have had a lot of success with using local AI for adding metadata to our files. Like many companies, we have terabytes of data on our network. Stardock develops both software and games and on the game side, there’s decades of 3D and 2D art assets, videos, work products, etc.

According to recent reports, around the company we have a lot of pretty decent video cards from AMD and NVIDIA. We have found that 8B to 12B parameter models are more than enough to do everything we need and those will run on even relatively older hardware. Right now, we have a Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 laptop doing some of this work in the background during the evening.

Local AI is really good at just slowly chewing through and reviewing these files and adding metadata to it so that when we need to find something, you can search for it and find it promptly. Hence, we discovered that we have 16 different 3D models of wolves. Sigh.

What should trigger escalation from a smaller local model to a more capable cloud model? How do you detect when the local model is struggling before it makes a consequential mistake?

Industry observers note that right now, anything that requires open-ended judgement should probably go up to the cloud. The frontier models have largely solved hallucinations. When you go to smaller (local) models, hallucinations return. So on local models we tend to need to keep a lot of guardrails on them.

According to recent reports, clairvoyance organizes agents as AI staff with persistent memory and ongoing assignments. What have you learned about preserving useful context over time without allowing outdated instructions, incorrect assumptions, or conflicting memories to accumulate?

In a recent development, under the covers, Clairvoyance stores its memories in a graph structure so when one thing updates, it tends to recursively trigger updates to other nodes. This helps ensure that the memories stay organized and up to date.

The challenge has been to prevent infinite recursion and that has required a lot of trial and error over the last couple of years.

Recent findings suggest that giving agents access to files, applications, and development tools makes them more useful, but also increases the consequences of errors. How do you structure permissions, human approvals, and recovery when an agent takes the wrong action?

The one concrete point we have is File Protection: Clairvoyance can block agents from wiping out directories, enforced at the app level rather than through hooks that an agent could work around.

In a recent development, when a workflow combines local execution with cloud inference, “local-first” can mean different things. What information leaves the user’s machine, and how can users understand and control that boundary?

Industry observers note that cloud security is about keeping other people out. It doesn’t answer whether the model provider should have your manufacturer’s secrets in the first place. Clairvoyance is local-first by design: your notes, projects, and staff memory live on your own machine. What goes to a cloud model is your call, made per staff member, not a blanket setting. Run a local model and nothing has to leave your hardware at all. We’re hearing this directly from enterprise customers who are frustrated about uploading entire confidential workflows to Anthropic or OpenAI just to get work done.

Clairvoyance has over 40,000 owners. What have you learned from how people actually use Clairvoyance, and can you share a measurable example of a recurring workflow where it has delivered sustained value?

The retention rate is highly dependent on the amount of data the user is generating through their sessions.

It has been revealed that most customers of AI haven’t really crossed the threshold where they are taking the data the AI generates to build back onto it. Most users still think in terms of prompts. The users who stay with Clairvoyance are the ones generating a lot of Exhibits and Reports which in turn act as the foundation for further work.

According to recent reports, looking ahead a year, what developments would most expand the work agents can reliably handle locally? What would need to happen for you to reconsider your view that routing matters more than model size?

I think within 18 months, 90 to 95% of AI work will be local, with maybe 5% needing the cloud for frontier work. That’s mostly because almost nothing is being delegated to AI yet, even trivial tasks like screening resumes for location or checking shipment timing are still done by hand, and a 4B model can already do that on a laptop. What expands this is Hivemind-style pooled compute (letting a manufacturer’s underused GPUs serve everyone on the domain) and routing getting good enough that nobody has to know what a 4B model or an Opus even is.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to try a desktop app for managing persistent AI agents across their computers should visit Clairvoyance AI.

As a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

Beyls: Wrapping up LLVM's relicensing effort

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (153 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lwn

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.
  • In a recent development, we've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018.
  • Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort.

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

In a recent development, we've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. Upcoming contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...].

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, every article on LWN.net is written for humans, by humans.
  • The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation of Android's Binder driver, the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices.
  • Binder was added to the kernel in 2008, Llamas mentioned, as an interprocess communication mechanism for Android devices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every article on LWN.net is written for humans, by humans. If you've enjoyed this article and want to see more like it, your subscription goes a long way to keeping the slop at bay. We are offering a free one-month trial subscription (no credit card required) to get you started.

The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation of Android's Binder driver, the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices. Carlos Llamas confirmed that he had deleted the C code to general applause, and then shared some insights about what went into replacing the C implementation. Alice Ryhl, who has worked on the Rust implementation for some years, added her own thoughts about what the most difficult and interesting parts of the transition were.

Binder was added to the kernel in 2008, Llamas mentioned, as an interprocess communication mechanism for Android devices. Its design originated in BeOS, but it has grown significantly since then. It provides a rich set of operations for allowing processes to communicate with the minimum amount of overhead. It also, therefore, presents a large attack surface for Android. Many complicated chained attacks against Android have involved Binder at one step or another, Llamas explained. Google's internal "red team" (the team dedicated to proactive security research) deemed Binder to be the most vulnerability-dense component in the entire operating system, with more CVEs per line than anywhere else.

It has been revealed that that made it an obvious candidate for porting to Rust, Llamas stated. Binder was the first user of Rust in the kernel, he added, although Ryhl did not publicly post the first version of what became the Rust implementation until 2023, well after the Rust experiment started in 2021. All told, the effort took more than five years. Binder is used for every single screen touch, permission check, and cross-application message on Android, which runs on more than three billion devices. In total, it works out to hundreds of billions of Binder transactions per second, globally, he added. That scale meant that even the smallest discrepancy between the interface provided by the C version and the one provided by the Rust version would cause problems and regressions for some use case.

Industry observers note that one particularly tricky aspect has been performance, Ryhl said. Throughput doesn't matter that much; what matters is the tail latencies. Most screen frames on Android have a Binder transaction in the critical path of the frame, she explained. So, a difference of two microseconds on average is not a real problem, but if Binder is ever twenty milliseconds slower, even once in a while, people will notice and care.

The actual algorithms that the C and Rust implementations use are identical, she continued, so there are no large differences in throughput. But, because Rust handles locking differently, there were problems with the tail latency from lock contention that she had to debug. For example, one user-reported traceback demonstrated Binder attempting to take a mutex that was held by another process. That process was preempted, and did not resume executing for twenty milliseconds, well past the sixteen millisecond budget to render a single frame.

Recent findings suggest that it was a classic case of priority inversion. To solve the problem in Binder, Ryhl moved as many operations out from under the lock as possible, and was able to replace it with a spinlock, which made the problem go away. The equivalent lock in the C implementation was already a spinlock: "I deviated from C Binder, and pow. It has eighteen years of accumulated quirks.".

Eventually, however, the Rust implementation was good enough for most use cases. And the C implementation was still producing upcoming vulnerabilities every time someone tried to introduce a new feature. Eventually, Llamas and Ryhl decided to only add new features to the Rust implementation, in order to motivate people to switch and to avoid headaches from the C implementation. That policy has resulted in the Rust version becoming faster than the C version, because Ryhl was able to introduce an algorithmic improvement that reduced the number of needed system calls, a change that had been considered too complex for the C implementation. Now that the C implementation has been deleted, there are more of those coming, she promised.

Another area that proved difficult was dealing with tracepoints. Users aren't supposed to rely on the presence or behavior of most kernel-internal tracepoints, but they do. This meant that Ryhl had to copy the existing tracepoints in Binder as a de facto part of the driver's API. That even extended into some of the data structures involved in the driver. In one case, she said, there was a reference-counted structure that had a slightly different reference count in the Rust implementation, because the Rust code was holding an additional pointer to the structure. That turned out to be a problem for one particular piece of client code, since it relied on checking the reference count via a tracepoint in order to determine when the C implementation had reached a particular state.

There was also a lot of toolchain support needed, Ryhl continued. The Rust implementation had to work with kernel address-space layout randomization (KASLR), control-flow integrity (CFI), and profile-guided optimization. Production Android kernels are built with all of those enabled, and since they impact code generation, the Rust code needed to account for them.

According to recent reports, llamas then went into more detail about the deployment initiative that will be used to convert customers to the Rust implementation. A major problem with just rolling the Rust implementation out is the existence of vendor hooks: custom tracepoints used to inject vendor-specific behavior into the kernel. The Rust implementation of Binder was not able to reproduce those in every case, and therefore many vendors are stuck on the C implementation until they enhancement their code. That's going to be a slow process.

According to recent reports, old stable versions of the kernel will continue to have the C Binder, and receive security fixes, which gives the various Android vendors a little bit of leeway until they're forced to patch. After the conference, the patch removing the C implementation was merged as part of the 7.4 merge window, so that is the version past which the Rust implementation is required. 7.3 is the designated long-term-support release for 2026.

It has been revealed that one person asked whether this would pose a problem for people compiling the kernel with GCC. Miguel Ojeda responded that many distributions are using a workaround for the current lack of Rust support in GCC: they are building the C side of the kernel with GCC, and the Rust side with LLVM. He remarked that he had advised against compiling the kernel in that way, because it is "a complete hack", though people who use it are unlikely to complain about being forced onto Clang. Greg Kroah-Hartman added that it will take months or years to learn about anyone who has problems with the Rust version of the driver, given how slowly Android vendors update their kernels. Furthermore, the removal is a single patch that can be cleanly reverted, if someone needs to continue using the C version.

Llamas thought that it was worth considering what the removal process should look like for other code that gets ported to Rust. He asked what people thought should happen to the C version of converted drivers on long-term-support branches. Ojeda said that the process would be exactly the same as the existing policy for replaced C code. The only difference between Rust and C in long-term-support releases is that the Rust maintainers backport fixes for soundness problems, he said. Kroah-Hartman told Llamas not to worry about code that has been replaced: "Just delete it. I take patches for subsystems that have been deleted. It's fine.".

It has been revealed that with that declaration, the session, the conference, and the presence of the C Binder driver in the kernel were all over. Binder is the first nontrivial component in the kernel to be ported to Rust, and its journey has revealed several pitfalls that don't apply to upcoming drivers written in Rust from scratch. Still, the most difficult problems were not Rust-specific; they were the compatibility problems that any rewrite would face. Whether any other kernel components will find the hassle of a rewrite worth it, and how long they will take to accomplish it, remains to be seen.

[ Thanks to the Linux Foundation, LWN's travel sponsor, for supporting my travel to Kangrejos. ].

This isn't a workaround, it's entirely normal. The C ABI is the same between GCC and LLVM. The only downside I'm aware of is that you can't do cross-language LTO this way.

It has been revealed that for the (large) subset of things that are standardized and ABI-defined, yes, but if there's e.g. an __attribute__((packed)) on a struct, using the same version of clang for your C compiler and for bindgen (in the form of libclang) can be expected to get it right, and there is no such expectation if it's two different compilers. And of course if you do something like enable a layout-changing plugin in GCC like randstruct, then this will definitely not work (though Kconfig prevents that particular mistake).

Industry observers note that it's equivalent to the reason that the standard advice is to use the exact same compiler for your kernel itself and for kernel modules. The ABI is supposed to be standard, but the kernel uses lots of language features and compiler-specific features.

(To be clear, I'm inclined to agree with you that it will generally work, and for over 20 years there has not actually been any enforcement that you did use the same compiler version.).

Sources indicate that aren't there codegen-affecting flags like CFI and such that are build options in the kernel? I imagine that needs compiler internal logic to match….

Aren't there codegen-affecting flags like CFI and such that are build options in the kernel? I imagine that needs compiler internal logic to match….

Codegen-affecting, yes, but are they ABI-affecting?

CFI is probably relaxed around anything that looks like an global-visibility symbol. What are other codegen-affecting options that involve nontrivial internal logic?

Other distributions like RHEL and SLES don't either. Is there a particular reason to single out Google here?

Sources indicate that I just bought a Samsung A27 (not a flagship), and Samsung promises 6 OS upgrades and 6 years of security updates. In this case (and probably others) the clock starts to run when a smartphone model appears globally, so it certainly is a good idea to look at the release year when comparing the patch promises of different smart phones.

If I search for 6 years of security updates, my favourite price comparison site lists smartphones from CMF, Honor, Motorola, Nothing, OnePlus, Oppo, Realme, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Xiaomi, so it's not just Samsung flagships. If you ask for 7 years instead, you get a different set of manufacturers (including Google); for 8 years, you get Fairphone. No one promises 9 or 10 years of security updates.

I previously had a Moto G100, gifted one year after it was released; it only had one more major Android release upgrade, and security fixes (which were already dripping at glacial pace) probably have finished too by now...

#69635. Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1395 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1395 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • Recent findings suggest that evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • Sources indicate that these arenas compare models by presenting owners with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

Recent findings suggest that evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

Sources indicate that these arenas compare models by presenting owners with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

In a recent development, while human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Industry observers note that our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

In a recent development, numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an important gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

In a recent development, you can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

Recent findings suggest that the “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

According to recent reports, the default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

The goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

We will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Complications and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

In a recent development, english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let people listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

In a recent development, human feedback remains an crucial part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as newly introduced TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Sources indicate that open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and customers better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

GitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

AI Can Scale Security. But Scale What?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that enterprise security teams today face more activity, telemetry and alerts than they can realistically investigate manually.
  • Industry observers note that for defenders, AI agents can change that equation by taking on investigations and other repetitive tasks across the environment.
  • Industry observers note that an agent investigating millions of endpoints must understand what it is looking for, what constitutes unusual behavior in that particular environment and which findings warrant further investigation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that enterprise security teams today face more activity, telemetry and alerts than they can realistically investigate manually. Estimates vary, with some research suggesting the average security operations team receives more than 4,400 alerts a day. As organizations expand and add more tools, and AI enables more attacks, that number is bound to grow. We’re already seeing examples of enterprises that have two million endpoints in their environment, and security teams that are investigating these alerts manually are not fighting a fair fight against attackers that are increasingly agentic.

Industry observers note that for defenders, AI agents can change that equation by taking on investigations and other repetitive tasks across the environment. However, the ability to process more data does not automatically translate into better threat detection or response. What’s needed is not just scale but context.

Industry observers note that an agent investigating millions of endpoints must understand what it is looking for, what constitutes unusual behavior in that particular environment and which findings warrant further investigation. Without this context, automation risks scaling noise and generating irrelevant or misleading conclusions.

And it’s important to keep in mind that not every organization will be able to rely on frontier model investigations for each alert; that will get far too costly.

According to recent reports, security environments differ in their infrastructure, applications, operational requirements, regulatory obligations and risk tolerance. Defenders must keep applications running while managing compliance requirements and avoiding operational disruption.

In a recent development, to be effective, agents must incorporate organizational knowledge, including historical investigations, established procedures and the judgment of experienced analysts. Much of this knowledge isn’t something that can just be fed to an agent in a spreadsheet or other format; it’s something that needs to be observed in action, by learning from experienced defenders at work.

For enterprises, the significant question here is how to take that institutional knowledge and translate it into systems capable of making consistent, contextually appropriate decisions at machine speed.

It has been revealed that organizations need mechanisms to capture and apply the knowledge that informs investigations, including previous case decisions, established procedures and how analysts interpret evidence. Enterprises may have “custom” types of processes, tools and tribal knowledge that need to be captured, as well.

Recent findings suggest that model specialization is one potential approach. Fine-tuning models for individual enterprise customers can support large-scale investigations at a more predictable cost while maintaining strong performance. Fine-tuned open-source models may be particularly useful for tasks involving very large endpoint populations.

Organizations must also evaluate agent performance as models, workflows and enterprise environments change. Synthetic environments, or digital twins, can provide representative settings for testing different agent versions when production data is no longer available or has become outdated.

Fine-tuning is not the only way to provide context. Retrieval, memory, workflow orchestration and explicit policy controls are alternative approaches. The central requirement is that the chosen method improves an agent’s performance in the environment where it will operate.

Correctly identifying a threat is only part of the challenge. Agents must understand which actions they are authorized to take, when human approval is necessary and how to avoid disrupting legitimate business operations. Determining where agents can act autonomously and where human decision-making is required is essential to trusted deployment.

Autonomy at scale also requires economy of scale. Companies that use frontier models for millions of investigations are going to bankrupt themselves. That makes finding the most efficient method of investigating with an AI model, whether a Small Language Model (SLM) or a proprietary one, paramount.

Recent findings suggest that autonomy should be proportionate to risk. Routine, well-understood tasks may be suitable for autonomous execution, while consequential or disruptive actions may require human approval or additional authorization. Enterprise security also depends on coordination across teams. An investigation that identifies a threat requiring a firewall configuration change must transition seamlessly to the team responsible for that system, with appropriate authorization and accountability for remediation.

Governance and workflow design are therefore essential components of agent deployment, not controls that can be added after the technology has been scaled.

Organizations should assess agents using outcome-based measures, including investigation accuracy, false-positive and false-negative rates, time to investigate and remediate, cost per investigation, escalation quality and adherence to authorization policies.

In a recent development, continuous evaluation is essential as models and workflows change. Testing different agent versions against representative cases and using synthetic environments can help organizations identify regressions before deploying updates into production.

Recent findings suggest that security leaders must balance the benefits of automation against the operational risks of deployment. Application availability, compliance obligations, organizational risk tolerance and implementation timelines all influence how quickly latest capabilities can be adopted.

AI offers security teams an opportunity to address a longstanding capacity problem, but raw scale is not the end goal. The real opportunity lies in combining machine speed with organizational context, appropriate authority and human judgment so agents can distinguish what matters, take the right actions and involve the right people when necessary.

Recent findings suggest that eyal Fisher is Co-Founder and CTO of Legion Security, where he leads the technical vision behind the firm’s agentic security operations platform. An AI thought leader and entrepreneur, Eyal previously co-founded generative AI company ART AI and a cloud security startup, and brings research experience from the University of Cambridge. A recognized pioneer in generative AI, he has spent his career pushing the boundaries of how machine learning can be applied to real-world security operations.

Tech Report: Announcing jj-musubi: live sync for Jujutsu

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Serpentine

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I’m pleased to announce a new source control tool, jj-musubi, that live-syncs copies of a Jujutsu (jj) repository across multiple machines.
  • jj-musubi makes repos on multiple machines feel like jj workspaces (worktrees if you speak git).
  • It’s intended for use by one person who works across several machines, so it has no security model (or rather, that is the extent of its security model).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I’m pleased to announce a new source control tool, jj-musubi, that live-syncs copies of a Jujutsu (jj) repository across multiple machines. Every time jj snapshots my work, jj-musubi syncs it to every machine in moments, and also commits, rebases, fetches, and so on.

This simple capability is surprisingly powerful.

jj-musubi makes repos on multiple machines feel like jj workspaces (worktrees if you speak git).

It’s intended for use by one person who works across several machines, so it has no security model (or rather, that is the extent of its security model).

Jujutsu already treats the working copy as a commit. Running jj status records a snapshot of my edits in that commit, which jj-musubi then syncs to my other machines. I like to have my shell prompt run jj status, so in practice I rarely have to think about snapshots.

Industry observers note that jj-musubi does not write to the working copy. Each machine has its own working copy and workspaces as usual, so syncs of commits, snapshots, and rewrites can bring in latest history while a build is running, without changing the files under it. On a laptop, I can work offline, and my machine will sync when I’m back on the network.

Sources indicate that this has also proven handy when I have agents working on several machines. I can give each agent its own jj workspace on different systems, then run jj diff -r devbox/agent-1@ on the laptop to see what one of them has done so far. If one finds a bug that another needs to fix, they can coordinate and see each other’s work without overhead.

jj-musubi refers to a collection of copies of a repo as a hive.

I often run agents in temporary disposable VMs. jj-musubi supports this by allowing an agent to lease its repo’s membership in the hive: if it doesn’t renew that lease in time, its repo gets forgotten about, so temporary repos or vanished containers can’t just stack up and clutter things.

Recent findings suggest that back when I was at Meta, I kicked off the project that became Sapling and Mononoke. Sapling’s Commit Cloud gives engineers there a similar way to move work between machines, and Google engineers have something similar with an internal jj server.

In a recent development, since then, I’d missed that everyday convenience for the machines I already use, and felt like I could get it without massive infrastructure or hosting. With jj-musubi, one machine runs a hub, and daemons exchange jj history with it over SSH. That’s almost as lightweight as you can get.

What’s tricky is getting concurrent work right. That’s already hard in any distributed source control system, and when syncs are live and we plan for disconnected work in an unreliable network, the difficulty goes way up.

As a user, I shouldn’t have to care about when exactly I can safely close my laptop after finishing an edit; all of my changes should make it through either just before I close it, or right after I reopen. No work should get lost or corrupted in the presence of interrupts, resends, delays, or machines sleeping, and the system should stay reliable even when machines go offline forever.

In a recent development, I used Lean to prove key properties of jj-musubi’s network protocol, and tests compare the Rust code against that model. An extensive body of other tests run real jj repositories through concurrent edits, interrupted syncs, hub restarts, and a myriad of other nasty situations. Mutation and adversarial testing ensure that when bugs are injected, sensible things happen. The safety guide details all the checks (and the parts I don’t yet cover).

It might sound spooky or dangerous to be able to see in-progress work on one machine from another. How can that be safe?

Recent findings suggest that if you use jj in multiple workspaces, you’re already used to the novelty of being able to check out the same change in two workspaces and modify it. jj simply marks the change as divergent, but it won’t update either working copy with changes from the other until you decide to, e.g. by calling jj workspace update-stale. In jj, dealing with divergent versions of a change is similar to any other kind of conflicted merge.

It has been revealed that jj-musubi uses jj’s existing workspace machinery, so everything will feel familiar. The only difference is that when you run jj-musubi, a workspace’s name is prefixed with the name of the machine it lives on.

Sources indicate that start with e.g. a laptop and another machine that’s always on (let’s call it devbox), with a copy of a jj repo on each. On each machine, download the binary or build it yourself:.

It has been revealed that run musubi hub on devbox; it will keep your sync data in ~/musubi-hub. In the laptop’s repo, run musubi create --hub devbox. In devbox’s repo, run musubi join.

I provide builds for Linux, macOS and Windows, and the quick start walks through setup and the first sync. If you try it and something surprises you, I’d like to hear about it.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • According to recent reports, the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • Industry observers note that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

According to recent reports, the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

Industry observers note that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates latest tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

Recent findings suggest that the specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

In a recent development, the user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Industry observers note that feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

In a recent development, realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

In a recent development, difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

Sources indicate that the verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

Consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Industry observers note that soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

It has been revealed that these properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

It has been revealed that given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

Sources indicate that autoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into newly introduced executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

Sources indicate that autoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

It has been revealed that we distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create fresh tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

The generator creates fresh tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

Recent findings suggest that the target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a fresh target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

It has been revealed that the multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

According to recent reports, to support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

In a recent development, together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

Generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

Recent findings suggest that the pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

For example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

According to recent reports, failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

According to recent reports, A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

Industry observers note that the controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

In a recent development, the useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

It has been revealed that after post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

It has been revealed that our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We plan to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

In a recent development, we use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

Recent findings suggest that the synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

Recent findings suggest that the training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

It has been revealed that we also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

The tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that companies are giving AI a bigger role in decisions, but that does not mean their leaders find decisions easier. In a survey published by Körber, 76% of senior decision-makers stated decision-making had become more complex. The same share reported allowing AI to play a greater role. The answers describe two trends happening at the same time; they do not establish that one caused the other.

Recent findings suggest that the survey included 2,000 senior executives, split evenly between the United States and Germany. Körber states respondents worked for organizations with annual revenue above $250 million and at least 250 employees, and fieldwork ran from August 27 to September 8, 2026. That makes the findings a look at decision-making inside larger organizations in two markets, not a representative measure of every employer or of small businesses.

The accompanying release notes 74% of respondents reported that information volume can get in the way of decisions, while 75% mentioned decisions stall when critical information is not available at the right time. Having more data and having the right data when a decision is due are different problems.

Recent findings suggest that consider a manager who needs to decide whether to delay a shipment. Sales, warehouse operations and finance may have different records for the same order, all updated at different times. An AI assistant can summarize those records rapidly, but a faster summary does not establish which number is current or who can approve an exception. Unless the team can check the sources and resolve conflicting records, the tool can move the work of reconciliation from one person to another rather than eliminate it.

The survey also found that 73% of respondents were uncomfortable letting technology make the final decision. That helps explain why businesses may want AI in the workflow without giving it control of the outcome. Drafting an explanation, gathering supporting documents and making a decision that commits the company are separate jobs. The cost of an error differs for each.

Sources indicate that among respondents whose organizations described their transformation as enterprise-wide, 63.8% reported strong organizational performance, compared with 41.6% of those at the pilot stage. Future-readiness confidence was 66.4% and 46.5%, respectively. Prepares to invest significantly in AI decision support were almost identical: 59% for the enterprise-wide group, versus 59.4% for the pilot group.

Sources indicate that those are self-reported group differences, not measured returns from a controlled rollout. Organizations that can implement technology across departments may already have stronger data, more resources or better operating processes. The publication does not establish that expanding a pilot causes performance to improve. It is better read as a prompt to ask what mature implementations do differently and which of those practices a particular team can test.

The practical question for an operator is where a tool improves the work between a question and a decision. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers a way to formalize responsibilities and decide what to measure in context. Teams can pick a recurring decision and compare how long it takes to obtain the necessary evidence, how often a recommendation must be corrected and whether an approver can explain what they relied on.

Tracking these measures separately can reveal a trade-off that a single adoption number misses. A tool may produce reports faster while increasing the time spent checking them, or it may let people spend less time gathering facts and more time evaluating options. For the executives surveyed, the challenge is not simply making AI more available. It is defining the role it plays when information is incomplete and someone still has to own the decision.

  • Industry observers note that A customer writes in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

In a recent development, figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

Industry observers note that A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

In a recent development, then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

In a recent development, final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

It has been revealed that the gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

Industry observers note that we use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

According to recent reports, starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

It has been revealed that table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

It has been revealed that claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

Sources indicate that one good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

It has been revealed that only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Industry observers note that figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Industry observers note that claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

Industry observers note that A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Sources indicate that capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

Industry observers note that we took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

It has been revealed that this is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

Sources indicate that A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Sources indicate that figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

Sources indicate that the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Recent findings suggest that now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

According to recent reports, we assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

Recent findings suggest that the practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Sources indicate that every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

In a recent development, at the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

It has been revealed that thinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

It has been revealed that the OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

According to recent reports, the useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

Latest Update: Databricks Brings PostgreSQL 19 to Lakebase and Neon
